headline: Online Casino Gambling Bill Passes as MPs Clash Over Fuel Security and Living Costs
summary: Parliament passed legislation to license online casino gambling during an extended sitting, after the Government argued regulation would improve oversight and opponents warned the scheme could expand gambling harm. Questions and annual reviews also exposed divisions over fuel-supply planning, a proposed liquefied natural gas import facility, rising household costs and welfare support. MPs advanced a Treaty settlement and debated proposed changes to environmental agencies and rules, while the Government defended its economic and energy approach against sustained criticism.

topicSummaries.topic: Fuel-Supply Planning and LNG Proposal Face Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Fuel availability and energy policy affect transport, household power bills, jobs and the cost of goods.
topicSummaries.content: The Government said New Zealand remained in phase one of its national fuel response plan, with no current supply disruption and importers confident about orders through May and June. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said detailed arrangements for prioritising “critical customers” in a severe shortage were still being worked through with industry. Opposition leader Chris Hipkins pressed for definitions and procedures, while Energy Minister Simeon Brown defended the proposed LNG import facility as a response to dry-year electricity risk and a shortage of domestic gas. Labour and the Greens questioned its cost, exposure to international price spikes and the lack of a clear alternative plan. Associate Energy Minister Shane Jones said about $20 million was being used to restore up to 100 million litres of fuel storage at Marsden Point; the Government said further decisions on a strategic fuel buffer were still to come.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Two months after the fuel crisis started, why can’t he tell New Zealanders who critical customers are, how they will access fuel, what the role of the fuel companies is going to be, and when we might get to that point—what the criteria are for if we do get to that point?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We have six trigger criteria that actually bring officials, industry, and Ministers together to make an assessment about where we should be with respect to phases.

topicSummaries.topic: Food Inflation Slows, but Grocery Prices Are Still Rising
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Slower inflation does not mean food has become cheaper, and household budgets remain under pressure from groceries and fuel costs.
topicSummaries.content: Labour questioned Finance Minister Nicola Willis over food-price promises and the latest figures. Willis said food prices rose 3.4 percent in the year to March 2026, compared with a 12.1 percent rise in the year to March 2023, and acknowledged that the fall in inflation was not a decrease in prices. She attributed the slower rate of increases to the Government’s approach and pointed to seasonal differences across products. In the social development review, Labour and the Greens also raised food-grant declines, benefit sanctions and hardship. Social Development Minister Louise Upston said the jobseeker target of 50,000 fewer recipients by 2030 was at risk, but cited 80,700 people moving from benefits into work during the year under review and said assistance should remain targeted and temporary.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Barbara Edmonds (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Therefore, is that a decrease in food prices since she took office?

topicSummaries.topic: Online Casino Gambling Bill Passes by 68 Votes to 54
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The new law will bring online casino operators under a licensing and enforcement system, while setting rules for consumer protection and community funding.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed the Online Casino Gambling Bill at its third reading, with National, ACT and New Zealand First supporting it and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposing it. The law allows up to 15 licences, requires licensed operators to take harm-minimisation and consumer-protection measures, bars gambling on credit and provides penalties of up to $5 million for serious or persistent breaches. The Government says some revenue will be returned to communities through the Lottery Grants Board and that advertising will be restricted. Opponents accepted that online gambling already occurs but argued the bill could grow the market without adequate safeguards, and questioned whether community returns would be guaranteed. Reviews of the regime are planned after it is in place.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Online casino gambling is already widespread, easily accessible, and currently unregulated. There is no recourse when things go wrong.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: In our view, the licences are far too many for New Zealanders to practically understand the controls that, we say, do not go far enough.

topicSummaries.topic: India Free-Trade Agreement Set for Signing on 27 April
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The agreement could change market access for New Zealand exporters and establish new temporary work-visa arrangements.
topicSummaries.content: Trade Minister Todd McClay said New Zealand and India had agreed to sign a free-trade agreement in New Delhi on 27 April. He said 95 percent of New Zealand exports would receive tariff elimination or reductions, with 57 percent duty-free from the start and 82 percent when fully implemented. The Government says the deal could create export opportunities and jobs; after signing, it will go through parliamentary scrutiny, including public hearings. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters challenged the agreement’s visa, international-student and investment provisions. McClay said it would allow 1,670 high-skilled Indian workers annually under a three-year visa, but would not automatically grant those workers the right to bring family members. He described the investment figure raised by Peters as aspirational and said the agreement obliges New Zealand to promote investment, not to invest a set sum.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: Why does the India FTA include an investment clause with a completely unrealistic and unachievable $34 billion target over 15 years, when no previous New Zealand FTA has ever done so?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Todd McClay (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The New Zealand Government, through the India free-trade agreement, has not taken on a commitment to invest an amount of money in India.

topicSummaries.topic: Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu Settlement Bill Advances After 15 Years
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The settlement acknowledges Crown breaches and provides redress intended to support the iwi’s cultural identity and future development.
topicSummaries.content: The House agreed to the second reading of the Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu Claims Settlement Bill, with speakers from across parties supporting its progress. Negotiations began in 2011, and the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations said delays included disputes over overlapping interests in the Hauraki area. The bill gives effect to a Crown apology and includes $5.5 million in financial and commercial redress, cultural redress and recognition of Te Aroha maunga. Select committee changes also address Waikato Regional Council’s access to flood-protection assets. The bill is expected to return for its third reading next month alongside other Hauraki settlement bills.

topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to Treaty references in legislation could affect how public agencies and future governments recognise Treaty responsibilities.
topicSummaries.content: Te Pāti Māori, Labour and the Greens criticised the Government’s review of Treaty clauses, arguing it could weaken legal protections and deepen divisions. Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour, answering for the Prime Minister, said the Government intended to clarify or remove some references as part of its coalition policy and argued that legal rules should be clear and accessible. Labour said the review lacked detailed impact analysis and could affect provisions including environmental protections. The dispute formed part of a wider political clash over whether ministers were prioritising constitutional questions while households faced cost-of-living and fuel pressures.

keyExchanges.speaker: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Why should New Zealanders trust the Prime Minister’s position on Te Tiriti when it shifts, dependent on what keeps this coalition together?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon David Seymour (ACT), answering for the Prime Minister
keyExchanges.quote: New Zealanders should trust the Prime Minister’s position on the Treaty because this Government has actually delivered for Māori

topicSummaries.topic: Environment Ministry Merger and Freshwater Rules Under Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed restructuring and changes to environmental rules could influence decisions on housing, infrastructure, water quality and climate resilience.
topicSummaries.content: Labour and the Greens questioned the planned merger of the Ministry for the Environment into a new Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport, citing staff reductions and concerns about environmental oversight. Environment Minister Nicola Grigg said the merger was intended to combine related functions and reduce duplication, while preserving environmental capability. MPs also debated freshwater quality, farm plans and climate adaptation. Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard opposed restoring some land-use restrictions, arguing that improved farm practices and technology could reduce impacts; Grigg said freshwater rules and limits to protect human health were being developed. Climate Change Minister Simon Watts said national flood mapping was underway, with initial maps expected by the end of 2026 or early 2027, and said legislation would require local adaptation plans in high-risk areas.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Rachel Brooking (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is she concerned—like the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment is—that we risk losing an independent voice for the environment?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Grigg (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Environmental capability is very much going to remain a core capability of this new agency.

conclusion: The House advanced major legislation, but the day’s debates left unresolved whether the Government’s market-led approach to energy, gambling and reform can adequately protect households, communities and the environment.
